title: Profitable on day one? Jason Cohen on what "profitable" really means for bootstrapped founders
summary: Jason Cohen argues that bootstrapped founders who claim day-one profitability are ignoring the cost of their own labor. He offers stricter tests (could you pay someone else to do your job, would a new owner be profitable) and reminds founders that almost every great company, including his own, took years to get there.

principles.text: You're not profitable if you couldn't afford to pay someone else to do your job.
principles.quote: If you couldn't afford to pay someone else to do the job that you are doing, you're not profitable yet.

principles.text: The strongest test: would the business stay profitable if sold to an operator who hires people to do all the work?
principles.quote: The company is profitable when it would also be profitable in that scenario.

principles.text: A practical bar: the business replaces what the job you quit paid, since the market already priced your time.
principles.quote: The market has already decided your time and skills are worth at least that; if the startup replaces it, it's fair (in my book) to call it profitable.

principles.text: Claiming 'profitable from day one' on a tiny revenue base costs credibility with experienced people.
principles.quote: when you say "I'm profitable" it's a turnoff, because it's actually bullshit, and anyone with a modicum of experience knows it.

principles.text: Lower your required income through lifestyle and location to reach ramen-profitability sooner; it's easier when young and unattached.
principles.quote: You can dramatically change that income requirement through lifestyle and location; this is why it can be easier to start a company when you're young and unattached and childless

principles.text: Businesses are not profitable on day one; slow starts are normal, even for companies that later make millions in profit.
principles.quote: It's just that businesses aren't profitable on day one. They're profitable later (if ever).
